paragraphs.text: This oolong comes from the [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is), on Fujian's northern border with Jiangxi. Oolong is [traced to this area](fujian:history), and its making is said to have spread from here to Anxi, to Guangdong and then to Taiwan. [Meizhan](yancha:meizhan) is a Fujian cultivar that came from Anxi and is also made as Wuyi rock tea. It is less famous than Rougui and Shui Xian and is not one of the four famous bushes. The record gives the Wuyi Mountains but no zone within them, so it [does not say how close to the core](wuyi-mountains:on-a-label) the bushes grew.

The tea dates from 1981, which gives it forty-five years. Wuyi tea is finished with a [charcoal roast](yancha:making) in several rounds, and that roast dries the leaf so it keeps. Medium and full roast tea is the kind [kept for years](yancha:ageing), because the heavier the roast, the longer the tea is said to stay good. Over that time the roast softens. Damp is the main danger to stored rock tea, so how it is kept matters as much as how long.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker liquor with less sharpness, the roast softened and the high aroma faded.
